name: Singer
title: Singer Sewing Machines: History, Models and Parts in the UK
description: Singer sewing machines in the UK: history since 1851, the famous Clydebank factory, vintage machines worth keeping, and parts and servicing.
intro: The most famous name in sewing, with a British story too: for nearly a century, Singer machines were made at Clydebank in Scotland.
cardText: History from 1851, Clydebank, vintage machines and parts.

sections.html: Isaac Merritt Singer and Edward Clark founded I. M. Singer & Co in the United States in 1851. Singer became one of the world’s first truly global brands, helped by instalment payments that let households buy machines over time.

Singer built a huge factory at Kilbowie, Clydebank, near Glasgow, in the 1880s. It became one of the largest sewing machine factories in the world and ran until 1980. The local railway station is still called Singer. That is why so many British homes still have a Clydebank-built Singer.

Older all-metal Singers, hand-crank, treadle and early electric models, are durable and repairable. Many sew straight stitch beautifully through heavy fabrics. Check the serial number to date your machine, and look for missing parts such as the bobbin case or shuttle before buying.

Today’s Singer range covers mechanical beginner machines, computerised models and heavy-duty machines. As with any brand, check the build, the buttonhole and parts availability for the specific model.

sections.h2: Classic Clydebank models to look out for
sections.html:
Many British-made Singers carry a K after the model number, for Kilbowie, the Clydebank works. Names you will see on the second-hand market include:

  • Singer 201K: a full-size straight-stitch machine with a reputation for a very even stitch and quiet running.
  • Singer 99K: a smaller “three-quarter size” machine, popular as a portable.
  • Singer 15K and 66K: workhorse domestic machines, often found in treadle tables or with hand cranks.
  • Singer 222K Featherweight: a compact, lightweight machine with a free arm, much loved by quilters.

Condition matters far more than model: a serviced 99K will out-sew a seized 201K.

sections.h2: Checking a vintage Singer before you buy
sections.html:
• Turn the handwheel by hand: it should move smoothly with no grinding or tight spots.
  • Check the bobbin case or shuttle and at least one bobbin are present; they are model-specific.
  • Look at the motor wiring on electric models. Perished rubber cables need replacing by a competent repairer before use.
  • Ask whether it has been serviced recently. A full clean and oil often brings an old Singer back to life.

Our used sewing machine guide has a longer checklist.

sections.h2: Parts and servicing for Singer machines
sections.html: Singer machines are among the makes PK Sewing Machines lists on its website. PKSM services and repairs domestic and industrial machines in Leicester and stocks needles, bobbins, feet and other parts. Send the model number to check a part before you buy. Leicester’s hosiery heritage means the city has deep machinery know-how.

faqs.q: Is an old Singer worth repairing?
faqs.a: Often yes. Many older all-metal Singers are robust and parts for common models are still available. A specialist can check and service it.
Many Singers sold in Britain were made at Clydebank, near Glasgow. A “K” after the model number (for example 201K or 99K) usually indicates a Kilbowie (Clydebank) machine.

faqs.q: Are old Singer sewing machines worth repairing?
faqs.a: Often yes. Older all-metal Singers are simple, strong and well supported for parts, so a service is usually cheaper than a new machine of similar quality.
